newsitem.title: USA: U.S. official gratified with wto telecom offers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. official gratified with wto telecom offers.

text.p: The United States is "gratified" with the more than two dozen new and improved offers made by countries to break a logjam on world trade talks to open global telecommunications markets, a senior U.S. official said Friday.

But the official, who requested anonymity, said the talks have not yet reached the "critical mass" the U.S. believes is essential for a successful conclusion to the World Trade Organization negotiations. The official, speaking to reporters by phone, did however hold out the possibility for an acceptable agreement by a deadline of Feb. 15.
"This is a lot further advanced as against last April. We just have some ways to go before we get there," said the official, adding that the talks have been moving closer to U.S. objectives.

Efforts launched in 1995 to reach a WTO telecommunications accord failed last April after the United States said initial offers from many participants -- especially Asian nations -- were not enough to make a balanced pact possible.
But last summer key countries agreed to make another run at the issue with the aim of getting an accord by Feb. 15 of this year.

The official said that 27 countries recently have informed the United States -- either formally or informally -- that they planned to improve their earlier offers or that they intended to put forward an offer for the first time.
"We have been gratified with the interest in improving offers," said the official.
The United States has three principles in the talks:
-- Cross-border access to a country's domestic telecom market through the resale of services.
-- The right to facilities-based market access through the ability to invest in telecom suppliers in the domestic economy.
"We are getting closer to those objectives," said the official.

The official also held out the prospect that the European Union and the United States could settle their differences over the definition of video services. Europe has said that it wanted to exclude video from the talks -- a stance opposed by the United States and other nations.

The official said that based on recent talks "it appears" the European Commission "has room to work with us on arriving at a solution to this problem. And assuming that's the case, it should not be a danger to the negotiations."

The official added that if the EC took on the position it adhered to some months ago, "that would be a serious concern to us. But we're hopeful that the problem can now be worked out because the commission has the authority to do that."
